evidence.quote: With this release, you can issue public certificates that you can export and access the certificate’s private key to securely terminate TLS traffic on any compute workload. This includes EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises hosts.
evidence.context:
# AWS Certificate Manager introduces public certificates you can use anywhere
Posted on: Jun 17, 2025
AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) announces exportable public certificates that you can use on any workload that requires a public TLS certificate, whether within AWS or outside. With this release, you can issue public certificates that you can export and access the certificate’s private key to securely terminate TLS traffic on any compute workload. This includes EC2 instances, containers, or on-premises hosts.
ACM customers can now affordably issue, manage, and automate public certificates for use with your AWS, hybrid, or multicloud workloads. Previously, ACM-issued public certificates could only be used with integrated AWS services, such as Amazon CloudFront. Now, during certificate request, you can mark the certificate as exportable for use outside of integrated services as well. You can procure these certificates within seconds once you complete the required domain validation to prove that you are authorized to receive the certificate.
The exportable public certificates are valid for 395 days and costs $15 per FQDN and $149 per wildcard name. You don’t need to sign up for bulk issuance contracts and you only pay once for the lifetime of the certificate. Network and security administrators can monitor and automate the use of these certificates through ACM’s certificate lifecycle CloudWatch events
headings: AWS Certificate Manager introduces public certificates you can use anywhere

facts.claim: In a Lambda rotation function, the createSecret step generates a new secret value and stores it as a new version with the staging label AWSPENDING; storing it in AWSPENDING helps ensure idempotency.

values.display: store it with the staging label `AWSPENDING`

evidence.title: Lambda rotation functions
evidence.quote: Next it calls [`put_secret_value`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.put_secret_value) to store it with the staging label `AWSPENDING`.
evidence.context: The method `createSecret` first checks if a secret exists by calling [`get_secret_value`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.get_secret_value) with the passed-in `ClientRequestToken`. If there's no secret, it creates a new secret with [`create_secret`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.create_secret) and the token as the `VersionId`. Then it generates a new secret value with [`get_random_password`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.get_random_password). Next it calls [`put_secret_value`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.put_secret_value) to store it with the staging label `AWSPENDING`. Storing the new secret value in `AWSPENDING` helps ensure idempotency. If rotation fails for any reason, you can refer to that secret value in subsequent calls. See [How do I make my Lambda function idempotent](https://aws.amazon.com/premiumsupport/knowledge-center/lambda-function-idempotent/). **Tips for writing your own rotation function**

facts.claim: In a Lambda rotation function, the finishSecret step moves the AWSCURRENT label from the previous secret version to the new version; Secrets Manager adds the AWSPREVIOUS label to the previous version so that the last known good version is kept.

values.display: retain the last known good version

evidence.title: Lambda rotation functions
evidence.quote: Finally, the Lambda rotation function moves the label `AWSCURRENT` from the previous secret version to this version.
evidence.context: Next, the Lambda rotation function tests the `AWSPENDING` version of the secret by using it to access the database or service. Rotation functions based on [Rotation function templates](reference_available-rotation-templates.md) test the new secret by using read access. ### **finishSecret**: Finish the rotation Finally, the Lambda rotation function moves the label `AWSCURRENT` from the previous secret version to this version. Secrets Manager adds the `AWSPREVIOUS` staging label to the previous version, so that you retain the last known good version of the secret. The method **finish\_secret** uses [`update_secret_version_stage`](https://boto3.amazonaws.com/v1/documentation/api/latest/reference/services/secretsmanager.html#SecretsManager.Client.update_secret_version_stage) to move the staging label `AWSCURRENT` from the previous secret version to the new secret version. Secrets Manager automatically adds the `AWSPREVIOUS` staging label to the previous version, so that you retain the last known good version of the secret. **Tips for writing your own rotation function** + Don't remove `AWSPENDING` before this point, and don't remove it by using a separate API call, because that can indicate to Secrets Manager that the rotation did not complete successfully. Secrets Manager adds the `AWSPREVIOUS` staging label to the previous version, so that you retain the last known good version of the secret.
